newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt launches plan to make desert bloom.
newsitem.headline: Egypt launches plan to make desert bloom.

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak on Thursday launched an ambitious and controversial plan to make the Western Desert bloom with water channelled from the Nile.
On the banks of the lake behind the Aswan High Dam, Mubarak detonated a symbolic explosion at the site of what Egypt says will be the biggest pumping station in the world.
Within about four years the water will wind its way across the Western Desert, irrigating at least 500,000 acres (200,000 hectares) of virgin land to be settled by millions of people.

"A new era is opening for Egypt -- the era when we break out of the confines of the narrow Nile valley," he said in what officials described as a message to the world. "The old valley can no longer hold all the people."
More than 60 million Egyptians live in the Nile valley and Delta, which make up only four percent of the country's land area. The rest of the country is arid desert.

Mubarak, who in 14 years as Egyptian leader has acquired a reputation for extreme caution, has raised eyebrows with his sudden enthusiasm for the project, which had lain dormant in dusty feasibility studies for more than 20 years.

The stimulus appears to have been the heavy rains in Ethiopia last year, which raised the level of the water in the High Dam lake to record levels in October and put the spotlight on how Egypt uses its limited quota of Nile water.
But some experts say they have reservations about the project, saying it could turn out to be an expensive failure.
The leader of the opposition Wafd Party said on Wednesday that the project needed careful study and that he was worried it might waste public money for political purposes.
Geologist Rushdi Said, who has held senior academic posts in Cairo and Berlin, told Reuters on Thursday that he had serious doubts about the viability of the irrigation scheme.
"Pumping water into the desert is not a great idea. It's very expensive and you can use the water much better by concentrating on the Nile valley," he said.
"The valley and the Delta are a godsend -- there's no better land in the world. The best plan is to move industry and housing into the desert and make the most of the valley for farming."
But Mubarak has dismissed all criticism of the project, saying it is either misguided or perverse.

"We have groups who oppose absolutely any step forward. Whenever someone says something, we (Egyptians) have to come out and say 'No, no, no' -- the forces that are against any development," he said in an interview on state television.
"There is enough water... We still have a surplus of water. We will modernise the methods of agriculture in the old (Nile) valley and we are already recycling drainage water," he added.

The Wafd Party leader, Fouad Serageddin, and many other Egyptians are also worried about the price tag for the project, which government newspapers say will cost 2.76 billion pounds ($810 million) in the first four years.
That could blow a hole in the government's budget deficit, which has shrunk to about 1.1 percent of gross domestic product -- a source of pride for its economic reform programme.

Prime Minister Kamal Ganzouri, explaining the project at the site of the Toshka pumping station on Thursday, said the water would travel 310 km (190 miles) along a canal, across the desert northwest towards the small settlement of Baris.

He dismissed the argument that too much of the water would evaporate, saying the loss would be about 300 million cubic metres (66 billion gallons) a year -- a fraction of the 55 billion cubic metres a year Egypt can take from the Nile.
The Egyptian government has already invited international contractors to apply to prequalify for the pumping station, which will lift 300 cubic metres a second.
Ganzouri said on Thursday the station would cost $300 million but newspapers have said the price will be two billion pounds ($590 million).
